extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, practitioners, and examiners working on AI-related inventions (JPO and CNIPA)
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative guidance on how the JPO and CNIPA examine AI- and software-related patent applications, covering eligibility, claim formats, novelty, inventive step, enablement/support and example case analysis. Intended to inform drafting and prosecution strategy across the two offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2(1) JPA: 'Invention' in this Act means the highly advanced creation of technical ideas utilizing the laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed subject-matter does not comply with this definition it is rejected (main paragraph of Article 29(1) JPA). The JP Guidelines, Part III, Chap.1,2.1 lists ineligible subject-matter not regarded as 'inventions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2.2 Chinese Patent Law: 'Invention' means any new technical solution relating to a product, a process or improvement thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A solution that does not adopt technical means to solve a technical problem and thereby does not achieve any technical effect in compliance with the laws of nature does not constitute an invention (see CNIPA Guidelines Part II, Chap.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of excluded/ineligible subject-matter (CNIPA / Article 25.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 25.1 Chinese Patent Law enumerates excluded subject-matter: scientific discoveries; rules and methods for mental activities; methods for diagnosis/treatment of diseases; animal and plant varieties; substances by nuclear transformation; certain designs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA Guidelines further give examples of 'mental activities' including mathematical theories, methods of conversion, rules/methods of games, methods of deduction/inference/operations, methods and systems of managing organization/business/economy, computer programs per se, and methods of presenting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim statement requirements (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the JPO the statement in the claims must comply with: an invention for which a patent is sought is disclosed in the description; an invention for which a patent is sought is clear; the statement for each claim is concise (Article 36(6)(i),(ii),(iii) JPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be consistent with the description; unclear or indefinite claim scope (e.g., when it's unclear whether 'module', 'model', 'neural network' mean 'program') can breach clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable claim formats (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant can claim as an 'invention of a method' (series of steps) or an 'invention of a product' (program, structured data, data structure, computer-readable recording medium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a program 'for causing a computer to execute step A, step B ...'; structured data / data structure (whether stored or not) is acceptable; computer-readable medium claims are acceptable if the claim makes clear which of (a) program itself, (b) recording medium, (c) system into which program is read is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable claim formats (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: CNIPA accepts process/method claims, system/apparatus claims (means-for-implementing-steps), computer apparatus (memory+processor), computer-readable storage medium, and computer program product claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In apparatus claims, each component is treated as a program module required to realize each step; program product claims include program/instructions that carry out steps when implemented by a processor.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO two-step approach to software-related eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine under JP Guidelines Part III Chap.1 whether the claimed subject-matter is a 'creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature'; if that does not resolve eligibility, determine according to the 'idea based on the standpoint of software' (JPHB Annex B Chap.1,2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention utilises a law of nature as a whole it may be statutory without considering whether implemented in software. If not, examine whether information processing by software is specifically implemented by using hardware resources (cooperation of software and hardware). Examiner assesses the claim 'as a whole' irrespective of some recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of structured data to a program (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner determines whether structured data or a data structure is equivalent to a program — i.e., whether the structure of the data specifies the processing of the computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured data/data structures are determined to be software when equivalent to a program; if not equivalent, they are not determined to be software. Determination follows whether information processing specified by the structure is specifically implemented using hardware resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic claim-as-a-whole test (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination shall take all contents described in a claim as a whole, analyze the technical means involved, the technical problems solved and the technical effects obtained, and apply Articles 2.2 and 25.1 Chinese Patent Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not separate technical features from algorithmic or business-rule features; if a claim as a whole contains technical features applying laws of nature to solve technical problems and obtains technical effects, it may be patentable even if it includes algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA factors for a 'technical solution'
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim is a technical solution (Article 2.2), consider technical means, technical problems, and technical effects as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of technical solutions: (a) programs executed to solve technical problems by controlling/processing external or internal objects; (b) programs improving internal performance of computer systems (reducing storage/transmission, improving speed); (c) big-data algorithms that mine internal associations in data to improve reliability/accuracy in a specific application field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty examination principles (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should understand a software-related invention as a whole; do not specify it by arbitrary sub-division. When examining novelty, consider claims, description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing. For sub-combination inventions, consider elements relevant to another sub-combination only to the extent they specify structure/function of the claimed sub-combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements relevant to 'another sub-combination' merely specify that other sub-combination and do not affect the claimed sub-combination's structure/function, they may be disregarded; if they do specify structure/function then they contribute to novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty examination principles (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty means the invention does not form part of the prior art (Article 22.2). Principles: (1) identify identical inventions or utility models based on same technical field/problem/solution/effects; (2) perform separate comparison of each claim to each single prior art item (no combination of multiple items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim contains algorithmic or business-method features, consider all features in the claim (technical and algorithmic) in the novelty comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment procedure (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the 'primary prior art' most suitable for reasoning; determine whether a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by using secondary prior art or common general knowledge, following steps (1)–(4) (JP Guidelines Part III Chap.2,3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should not treat combination of multiple independent prior art items as the primary prior art. Steps include assessing factors supporting non-existence/existence of inventive step and comprehensively assessing supporting factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No technical/non-technical feature distinction in inventive step (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the inventive step assessment the JPO makes no formal distinction between features which are technical and those which are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed invention should be specified and compared as a whole against prior art; the standard reasoning process described (primary/secondary prior art approach) applies irrespective of feature 'technicality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment procedure (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step approach: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine the distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art by assessing whether the prior art provides technical motivation to apply those distinguishing features to the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances where technical motivation usually exists include: (i) distinguishing feature is common general knowledge; (ii) distinguishing feature is a technical means related to the closest prior art (e.g., disclosed elsewhere in same document with same function); (iii) distinguishing feature is a relevant technical means disclosed in another reference whose function is the same in solving the re-determined technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / Sufficiency of disclosure general requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Description must set forth the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete so that a person skilled in the art can carry it out (JPO Article 36(4)(i) / CNIPA Article 26.3 etc.). Claims must be supported by the description (support requirement, JPO Article 36(6)(i) / CNIPA Article 26.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient disclosure or lack of support for claimed scope can lead to refusal; examiners evaluate whether the description plus common general technical knowledge enable the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-specific enablement requirements (training data / model disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: For AI-related inventions, disclosure should include sufficient information about training data, model construction, and evidence of reliability/technical effect; model estimation results alone typically do not substitute for experimental verification unless the description enables a skilled person to reproduce and achieve the claimed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a trained model's estimation that a composition meets specified curing-strength characteristics is insufficient without experimental verification or clear instructions enabling reproduction; CNIPA and JPO both expect either concrete experimental data or disclosure that allows a skilled person to reproduce the model/result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement / No undue generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not generalize beyond what the description discloses; broad generalizations unsupported by disclosed embodiments are not allowed (support requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from CNIPA: Claim generalizing correlations beyond those recorded in description (different types of allergic reactions) was held unsupported. Remedies include amending claims to the specific disclosed mode (deleting broader claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer program products
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer program products should be regarded as software products that implement the solutions primarily through computer programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO: program products are software products; CNIPA: program/product claims are acceptable if the program/instructions can carry out the recited steps when implemented by a processor. Examiners assess whether such claims constitute technical solutions under applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting and unity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one independent claim is acceptable as long as those claims meet the requirement of unity (JPO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to maintain unity and clarity; for software-related inventions ensure each independent claim meets unity and is supported by the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination focus on solution defined by each claim (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination shall focus on solutions for which protection is sought, i.e., solutions defined by each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim includes both algorithmic and technical features, analyze whether the claim as a whole defines technical means solving a technical problem and providing technical effects; separate treatment of features is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA acceptance of supplementary experimental data
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3.5, Chapter 10, Part II, CNIPA Guidelines: examiners shall examine supplementary experimental data submitted after filing; the technical effect proved by such data should be available to a person skilled in the art from the contents disclosed in the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether supplementary data is accepted depends on the specifics; data submitted after filing cannot introduce technical effects that are not derivable from the original application contents.
